guide.title: Ripa, Rome: the Forum Boarium, the Circus Maximus, the Aventine and the Tiber island
guide.intro: Ripa is R. XII, Roma Capitale toponymic code 112, in Municipio I. It is the left bank of the Tiber below the Capitoline, and it takes in the whole of the Aventine hill. It has four distinct parts. In the Forum Boarium, two Republican temples, two late-antique arches and a twelfth-century basilica stand on and around one square, and the marble disc called the Bocca della Verita is in that basilica's pronaos. The Circus Maximus fills the valley between the Palatine and the Aventine. On the Aventine itself are Santa Sabina, the walled orange garden inside the Savelli fortress ground, and the keyhole on piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta. And the Isola Tiberina belongs to Ripa, as it.wikipedia's article on the rione states. San Saba and Testaccio were carved out of Ripa in 1921. The rione's arms are a white ship's rudder wheel on red, in memory of the river landing that named it.

sections.heading: The edges of Ripa, and the name
sections.body:
Almost every edge of this rione is a street or a square shared with a neighbour, and it.wikipedia's article on the rione names them: piazza di Monte Savello with Sant'Angelo; via del Teatro di Marcello, vico Jugario, via dei Fienili, via di San Teodoro and via dei Cerchi with Campitelli; piazza di Porta Capena with Celio; viale Aventino, piazza Albania and via e largo Manlio Gelsomini with San Saba; via Marmorata and piazza dell'Emporio with Testaccio; and the Tiber itself at lungotevere Aventino and lungotevere dei Pierleoni. A street named as a boundary is evidence of a line, not of what stands on either side of it.

Several things a visitor would file under Ripa fall on the far side of one of those lines. The Colosseum is in Celio; the Teatro di Marcello, the Portico d'Ottavia and San Nicola in Carcere are Sant'Angelo's. it.wikipedia's rione article lists the square in front of Santa Maria della Consolazione under Ripa. Ponte Sublicio is not Ripa's: Turismo Roma states that the present bridge joins the rioni of Trastevere and Testaccio at Porta Portese. it.wikipedia's article on Celio names piazza di Porta Capena as the boundary of Celio, San Saba and Ripa together. Via Marmorata is a boundary street, and the Arco di San Lazzaro stands on it. Piazza Albania is San Saba's, while the Scatola Archeologica addressed on it is Ripa's, which is the ordinary way a building and the square it opens onto can fall on different sides of a line.

One more thing is worth knowing because it looks like a contradiction. The rione is named for Ripa Grande, the river landing, and carries a rudder wheel in its arms for the same reason, but the landing itself stood on the far bank. This stretch of the Tiber was called Ripa Graeca, for the Greek community, the Schola Graeca, settled here from the fourth century and thickened in the eighth by Greek-Latins fleeing the iconoclasm of Leo the Isaurian. That name explains the church too: Santa Maria in Cosmedin takes its title from the Constantinople monastery Kosmidion, invoked by the Greek corporation entrusted with it.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route for this rione, so none is given here, and neither are walking times or distances. Steer by addresses, which for Ripa fall into four groups.

The Forum Boarium and the Velabro are addressed on three streets. Santa Maria in Cosmedin and the Bocca della Verita in its pronaos are at Piazza della Bocca della Verita 18; the Tempio di Ercole Vincitore, the Tempio di Portuno and the Fontana dei Tritoni stand on the same square. The Arco di Giano, the Arco degli Argentari and San Giorgio in Velabro are on via del Velabro, as is Rhinoceros at Via del Velabro 9, 00186 Roma. The Casa dei Crescenzi is on via Luigi Petroselli at the corner with via di Ponte Rotto, and the Palazzo dell'Anagrafe is at Via Luigi Petroselli 50. Sant'Omobono and its sacred area are on vico Jugario at the foot of the Capitoline.

For the Circus Maximus, the Circo Maximo Experience sells tickets on viale Aventino at the circus, and the Mitreo del Circo Massimo lies under a building on via dell'Ara Massima. The ex Pastificio Pantanella is on via dei Cerchi. The Monumento a Giuseppe Mazzini stands on piazzale Ugo La Malfa, on the Aventine slope facing the circus.

On the Aventine, Santa Sabina and the Giardino degli Aranci share Piazza Pietro d'Illiria; Santi Bonifacio e Alessio is on piazza di Sant'Alessio; the Villa del Priorato di Malta is at Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta 3-4, with Santa Maria del Priorato at number 4 and Sant'Anselmo on the same square. Santa Prisca is at Via di Santa Prisca 11 and the mithraeum beneath it at Via di Santa Prisca 8. The Roseto di Roma Capitale gives its address as Clivo dei Publicii 3 and via di Valle Murcia 6, and the Scatola Archeologica is on piazza Albania. On the island, San Bartolomeo is on piazza di San Bartolomeo all'Isola and the hospital at Via di Ponte Quattro Capi 39. The Kolbe Hotel Rome is at Via di San Teodoro 48.

sections.heading: Opening hours and tickets
sections.body:
Santa Sabina publishes the fullest timetable in the rione on its own site: visiting Sunday and Monday 12.00-19.00, Tuesday to Saturday 08.00-19.00, with days of precept running as Sundays. Entry is free and no booking is needed, visits are not permitted during liturgical celebrations, and the excavations are not accessible.

For Santa Maria in Cosmedin, Turismo Roma gives the visiting hours as every day 09.30-13.00 and 14.00-17.50, and advises confirming on 06 6787759 or with the basilica. The Divine Liturgy is celebrated on Sundays at 10.30 and the basilica is closed on 1 January. Those are also the hours for the Bocca della Verita, which stands in the pronaos. Santa Prisca's mass times, as Turismo Roma publishes them, are weekdays 08.00 and 18.00 and Sundays and feasts 08.00, 10.30, 12.00 and 18.00 in winter, and weekdays 08.00 and 19.00 and Sundays and feasts 08.00, 10.30 and 19.00 in summer. At San Bartolomeo all'Isola the Memoriale dei Nuovi Martiri opens on Saturday 09.30-13.30 and 15.30-17.30, and otherwise by booking through the basilica.

The Circus Maximus archaeological area opens Tuesday to Sunday: from late October to late March 09.30-16.00, last entry 15.00; from late March to late October 09.30-19.00, last entry 18.00. Tickets are sold through Vivaticket and on 060608. The Circo Maximo Experience, the augmented-reality route through the circus, runs 2 January to 31 May 10.00-16.00, 2 June to 31 July 17.00-21.00, 1 to 9 August 17.30-20.30, 11 to 23 August 17.00-20.00, 25 August to 13 September 16.30-19.30, 15 to 30 September 16.00-19.00, 1 October to 23 December 10.00-16.00, and 24 and 31 December 10.00-14.00, closed Mondays, 1 May and 25 December. Tickets are 12.00 euro full and 10.00 euro reduced, with a 22.00 euro family ticket for two adults plus under-18s bookable only through 060608 or a Tourist Infopoint.

Three more have conditions rather than hours. Turismo Roma states that the Roseto di Roma Capitale generally opens for the spring flowering from late April into May and again in October, with the calendar set each year. The Mitreo di Santa Prisca is not open: Turismo Roma states that visits are temporarily suspended and advises checking the official site. The library and archive in the Casa dei Crescenzi are open by appointment only, by email at least a week ahead, on 06 6798075. Trattoria Sora Lella on the island gives lunch Monday to Saturday 12.30-14.50 and dinner Monday to Saturday 19.20-22.50, closed Sunday, with telephone bookings and a stated dress code. For everything else, no source states opening hours, so none are given.

faq.question: Is the Colosseum in Ripa?
faq.answer: No. The Colosseum stands in the rione Celio. The Roman entertainment building Ripa does hold is the Circus Maximus, a chariot-racing circus 600 m long by 140 m wide in the valley between the Palatine and the Aventine, whose archaeological area is ticketed and open Tuesday to Sunday.

faq.question: Where is the Bocca della Verita and what does it cost?
faq.answer: It is the marble disc in the pronaos of the basilica of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, Piazza della Bocca della Verita 18, and it has stood there since 1632. Turismo Roma gives the visiting hours as every day 09.30-13.00 and 14.00-17.50 and advises confirming on 06 6787759 or with the basilica; the basilica is closed on 1 January. No source states an admission price. The disc is about 1.80 m across and is probably a Roman drain cover; the name is first recorded in 1485.

faq.question: Can you go inside the Circus Maximus?
faq.answer: Yes. The archaeological area opens Tuesday to Sunday, 09.30-16.00 with last entry 15.00 from late October to late March and 09.30-19.00 with last entry 18.00 from late March to late October, with tickets through Vivaticket and on 060608. Investigations concluded in 2016 opened lit visitor routes through the galleries that led to the cavea, and an internal stair in the Torre della Moletta reaches a viewpoint over the area. Separately, the Circo Maximo Experience is a ticketed augmented- and virtual-reality route of about 40 minutes with nine stops, in eight languages.

faq.question: What is the keyhole on the Aventine?
faq.answer: It is the hole in the portal at Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta 3, which frames, at the end of an avenue of trees, the dome of St Peter's. The complex of buildings and garden behind it is the historic seat of the Grand Priory of Rome of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta and houses the Order's embassy to the Italian State. Turismo Roma credits the square's present appearance to Giovanni Battista Piranesi, commissioned in 1764 by Cardinal Giovanni Battista Rezzonico.

faq.question: Is the Isola Tiberina in Ripa, or in Trastevere?
faq.answer: In Ripa. it.wikipedia's article on the rione states that the Isola Tiberina belongs to Ripa. Its two bridges reach two other rioni: ponte Fabricio, of 62 BC, lands on the left bank in rione Sant'Angelo, which Turismo Roma names, and ponte Cestio, of about 46 BC, carries the other side to Trastevere. On the island itself stand the basilica of San Bartolomeo, the Sacconi Rossi oratory, the hospital and one trattoria.

faq.question: Is the port of Ripa Grande in this rione?
faq.answer: No. The rione takes its modern name from the river landing and carries a white rudder wheel on red in its arms in memory of it, but the landing itself stood on the far bank of the Tiber. What Ripa holds of the river is its four bridges, the Cloaca Maxima outfall at lungotevere Aventino, and the island.

photos.title: Tempio di Ercole Vincitore, Forum Boarium
photos.description: The circular marble temple of Hercules Victor of about 120 BC, standing on the piazza della Bocca della Verita in the Forum Boarium.
photos.author: ChromosomeGun

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Cosmedin
places.address: Piazza della Bocca della Verita 18, Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica on the piazza della Bocca della Verita, whose pronaos holds the marble disc of that name. Interior of three naves on four piers and eighteen antique columns, with a Cosmatesque pavement, fragments of eighth- and ninth-century frescoes, a schola cantorum built under Callixtus II and a Gothic-Florentine ciborium by Deodato of 1294. Turismo Roma gives the visiting hours as every day 09.30-13.00 and 14.00-17.50, and advises confirming on 06 6787759 or with the basilica. The Divine Liturgy is celebrated on Sundays at 10.30. The basilica is closed on 1 January.
places.history: First recorded in the sixth century as Sancta Maria in Schola Graeca, with the rank of diaconia, and enlarged in 782 by Pope Hadrian I over the Ara Maxima of Hercules, whose Aniene-tufa core still stands in the rear half of the church and inside which the crypt was cut. It took its present form in the twelfth century, after the damage of Robert Guiscard's invasion; the portico and the seven-storey Romanesque campanile of bifore and trifore, 34.20 m tall with a bell of 1289, are the work of Alfano Camerario. The name comes from the Constantinople monastery Kosmidion, invoked by the Greek corporation entrusted with the church, which is also why the surrounding area was called Schola Graeca and this bank of the Tiber Ripa Graeca.

places.name: Bocca della Verita
places.address: Piazza della Bocca della Verita 18, Roma RM
places.summary: A marble disc roughly 1.80 m across, set in the pronaos of Santa Maria in Cosmedin since 1632 and sharing that basilica's visiting hours. It carries a bearded male face, read as Jupiter, a faun or a river god, with the eyes, nose and mouth pierced, flanked by a scarab, two pincers and two wolf heads.
places.history: The disc is probably a Roman drain cover from the reign of Tarquinius Superbus, who built the Cloaca Maxima. The name dates from 1485 and attaches to the medieval story that the mouth would bite the hand of a liar. William Wyler's Roman Holiday, of 1953, put it into the tourist imagination.

places.name: Tempio di Ercole Vincitore
places.address: Piazza della Bocca della Verita, Roma RM
places.summary: A circular temple of marble on the piazza della Bocca della Verita, in the Forum Boarium, of about 120 BC. Also called Ercole Invitto or Ercole Oleario.
places.history: A Renaissance misattribution still has it popularly called the Temple of Vesta, because its round plan resembles the Temple of Vesta in the Roman Forum. The building later served as the church of Santa Maria del Sole; with the recovery of the ancient monument the church was deconsecrated.

places.name: Tempio di Portuno
places.address: Piazza della Bocca della Verita, Roma RM
places.summary: A small rectangular temple to Portunus, god of river harbours, also known as the Tempio della Fortuna Virile, standing in the Forum Boarium by the ancient Portus Tiberinus. High podium with steps faced in travertine slabs, four Ionic columns on the front, and two travertine columns with five Aniene-tufa half-columns on the cella walls. Turismo Roma states that the building is visible from the outside.
places.history: Datable to the fourth or third century BC, though the present fabric is probably of the second half of the second century with first-century-BC reworking. Byzantine-era frescoes of the life of Mary survive inside. In the ninth century it became a church, first Santa Maria de Gradellis, or de Secundicerio, and from the fifteenth century Santa Maria Egiziaca, a title it kept until 1916, when the church was deconsecrated and the ancient temple restored.

places.name: Fontana dei Tritoni
places.address: Piazza della Bocca della Verita, Roma RM
places.summary: A fountain on the piazza della Bocca della Verita whose main basin is an octagon with concave sides, echoing the eight-pointed star of the Albani arms. Two kneeling tritons carved by Francesco Moratti hold an oyster-shaped shell, and two further Albani coats of arms sit on the outer rim.
places.history: The foundation stone was laid on 11 August 1717, to a design by Carlo Francesco Bizzaccheri for Pope Clement XI Albani, drawing on Bernini's Triton fountain in piazza Barberini for both subject and manner. Four mascherone heads on the basin rim were removed in the nineteenth century. An adjoining public trough, built by the same pope for citizens and cattle, was dismantled in the early twentieth century during the Tiber embankment works and moved to lungotevere Aventino.

places.name: Piazza Bocca della Verita
places.address: Piazza della Bocca della Verita, Roma RM
places.summary: The square that occupies the ground of the Forum Boarium's ox market. It gathers Santa Maria in Cosmedin, the Temple of Hercules, the Temple of Portunus and the Fontana dei Tritoni.
places.history: Archaeological finds of eighth-century-BC Greek ceramic and Mycenaean fragments confirm the tradition of contact with Greece and Asia before the foundation of Rome. Capital sentences were carried out here until 1868.

places.name: Foro Boario
places.address: Via Luigi Petroselli, Roma RM
places.summary: The cattle-market district between the Tiber, the Capitoline, the Palatine and the Aventine, with the Republican temples of Portunus and Hercules Victor facing the river. Turismo Roma describes it as an area open to the public.
places.history: The ground was anciently occupied by the Velabrum marsh, drained by the Etruscan kings in the sixth century BC with the building of the Cloaca Maxima, whose arches are still visible. The Portus Tiberinus, ascribed to Servius Tullius in the same century, lay where the Anagrafe offices now stand. Imperial works here include Trajanic warehouses, of AD 98-117, by the river port, the Arch of the Argentarii of AD 204 and the four-fronted arch of Janus, probably of the time of Constantius II, AD 337-361.

places.name: Arco di Giano
places.address: Via del Velabro, Roma RM
places.summary: A four-fronted arch on via del Velabro, square in plan, on four piers under a groin vault carrying a high attic, built in brick faced with marble, much of it spoil. Two rows of three niches on each pier originally held 48 statues; only the four female figures on the keystones survive, read as Roma, Juno and perhaps Minerva and Ceres. Turismo Roma states that it is always visible from the outside. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The last monumental building put up in the eastern Forum Boarium. The name is a sixteenth-century misnomer: the arch is probably the Arcus Divi Constantini of the fourth-century Regionary Catalogues, built by Constantine's sons in his honour after his death. In the Middle Ages the Frangipane used it as the base of a tower. Partly buried for centuries, it was fully uncovered in 1827, when the attic was demolished.

places.name: Arco degli Argentari
places.address: Via del Velabro, Roma RM
places.summary: Not an arch but a trabeated gateway about six metres high, adjoining the flank of San Giorgio in Velabro on via del Velabro. Travertine base, otherwise faced entirely in white marble, with acanthus scrolls and military standards on the piers, Victories and eagles on the capitals, and sacrifice scenes, soldiers and barbarian prisoners.
places.history: Erected in AD 204, paid for by the guild of money-changers and cattle merchants, the argentarii et negotiantes boarii, and dedicated to Septimius Severus, Julia Domna and Caracalla. The names of Fulvia Plautilla and Geta were chiselled out of the dedicatory inscription; the principal reliefs inside show Severus and Julia Domna on one side and Caracalla on the other, with Geta, Plautilla and probably Plautianus erased under the damnatio memoriae. In the seventh century its eastern pier was half-swallowed by the wall of San Giorgio. The many drill holes in the monument are traditionally ascribed to medieval treasure-hunters.

places.name: Chiesa di San Giorgio in Velabro
places.address: Via del Velabro, Roma RM
places.summary: A church on the piazzetta della Cloaca Massima, with the Arch of the Argentarii built against its flank and the so-called Arch of Janus on the same street. It lies within the parish of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli and is a rectory entrusted to the Order of the Holy Cross. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The result of a ninth-century enlargement of an earlier diaconal building, much altered since. It is the seat of the diaconate of San Giorgio in Velabro, whose cardinal deacons have included the future popes Boniface IX, from 1381 to 1385, and Martin V, from 1406 to 1417, and St John Henry Newman, from 1879 to 1890. Pope Gregory II, who reigned from 715 to 731, made it the station church of the Thursday after Ash Wednesday.

places.name: Cloaca Massima
places.summary: Rome's ancient main drain, whose outfall is the part of it that belongs to this rione. Turismo Roma records it as still functioning where it discharges on the left side of Ponte Palatino, at lungotevere Aventino.
places.history: Built at the end of the sixth century BC under Rome's last kings, using Etruscan vaulted-arch engineering. It runs from the Suburra by the Argiletum, the Forum, the Velabro and the Forum Boarium to the Tiber. Its arches are still visible in the Forum Boarium, the marsh ground it was dug to drain.

places.name: Casa dei Crescenzi
places.address: Via Luigi Petroselli, Roma RM
places.summary: An aristocratic house of the eleventh or twelfth century on via Luigi Petroselli, at the corner with via di Ponte Rotto, facing the Temple of Portunus; Turismo Roma places it in the rione Ripa. Two storeys survive, the ground floor and part of the upper, incorporating spoil from Roman buildings: volutes, coffers, putti, sphinxes. It is now the seat of the Centro di Studi per la Storia dell'Architettura, whose library and archive are open by appointment only, by email at least a week ahead, on 06 6798075.
places.history: A long inscription on the side elevation records that it was built not for vainglory but to renew the ancient dignity of Rome, by Nicola, son of Crescenzio and Teodora, for his son Davide. The position let the family watch traffic on the Tiber and across Ponte Emilio, on which they levied a toll. It is also known as Tor Crescenzia, as the Casa di Cola di Rienzo and as the Casa di Pilato. Abandoned in the fifteenth century and later used as a stable and hayloft, it was bought by the papal government in the later nineteenth century and ceded to the Comune. The Centro, founded by Gustavo Giovannoni, dates the handover to 25 February 1939, after restoration by G. Petrignani.

places.name: Palazzo dell'Anagrafe
places.address: Via Luigi Petroselli 50, Roma RM
places.summary: The registry building of the Governatorato di Roma, on via Luigi Petroselli, put up on the site of the hospice of Santa Galla and its old church. The medieval quarter of the Forum Boarium was demolished in 1936 and replaced with public-administration buildings.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on the rione gives the construction dates as 1936 to 1939, names Ignazio Guidi and Cesare Valle as its designers and the Impresa Tudini e Talenti as contractor. Turismo Roma adds Vincenzo Fasolo, working on Valle's drawings. The Centro di Studi per la Storia dell'Architettura, in the Casa dei Crescenzi, records that Valle designed the adjoining municipal office buildings in 1936, with brick elevations chosen to chime with the medieval house.

places.name: Chiesa di San Giovanni Decollato
places.address: Via di San Giovanni Decollato, Roma RM
places.summary: A church on the street of the same name, seat of the Arciconfraternita di San Giovanni Decollato. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The confraternity seated here accompanied those condemned to death in Rome.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Omobono
places.address: Vico Jugario, Roma RM
places.summary: A church on vico Jugario, at the foot of the Capitoline, standing at the edge of the archaeological area that carries its name. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records it as a Catholic church of Rome in the rione Ripa.

places.name: Area sacra di Sant'Omobono
places.address: Vico Jugario, Roma RM
places.summary: An archaeological area on vico Jugario at the foot of the Capitoline, named for the church of Sant'Omobono, containing two temples: the temple of Fortuna and the temple of Mater Matuta. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The area was discovered in 1937. Excavation produced material from archaic and republican Rome.

places.name: Circo Massimo
places.summary: The Roman chariot-racing circus in the Valle Murcia, the valley between the Palatine and the Aventine, 600 m long by 140 m wide. The archaeological area opens Tuesday to Sunday: from late October to late March 09.30-16.00, last entry 15.00; from late March to late October 09.30-19.00, last entry 18.00. Tickets are sold through Vivaticket and on 060608. Visitors can walk the galleries that led to the cavea and follow the ancient paving past rooms that held shops, inns and small offices. Turismo Roma reads the present garden layout as the plan of the circus: the grassed slope for the terraces, the beaten earth for the track, the long central bed for the spina, with the Domus Augustana on the Palatine above.
places.history: Under the Tarquins the valley was already used for chariot racing; a masonry circus proper came with Julius Caesar. Racing teams ran under colours, green, blue, red and white, and the crowd divided on the terraces by the colour of their favourites. The space also served triumphs, processions and public executions. An obelisk brought to Rome in 357 stood here and is now at the Lateran. Repeatedly destroyed by fire, the circus was rebuilt almost entirely under Trajan, to which phase most of the visible structures belong. It stayed in use into the first decades of the sixth century, then became farmland, and in the modern period carried gasworks, warehouses, manufactories, workshops and housing until the early 1900s and the passeggiata archeologica.

places.name: Circo Maximo Experience
places.address: Viale Aventino, Roma RM
places.summary: A ticketed augmented- and virtual-reality tour of the Circus Maximus in its historical phases, using see-through visors and stereo headsets included in the ticket. A route of about 40 minutes with nine stops, in eight languages, Italian, English, French, German, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Japanese, with the voices of Claudio Santamaria and Iaia Forte. Tickets are 12.00 euro full and 10.00 euro reduced; the 22.00 euro family ticket, for two adults plus under-18s, is bookable only through 060608 or a Tourist Infopoint. Tickets are also sold on site, and arrival 15 minutes before the booked slot is advised, with no refund or reslotting for latecomers.
places.history: The 2026 timetable runs 2 January to 31 May 10.00-16.00; 2 June to 31 July 17.00-21.00; 1 to 9 August 17.30-20.30; 11 to 23 August 17.00-20.00; 25 August to 13 September 16.30-19.30; 15 to 30 September 16.00-19.00; 1 October to 23 December 10.00-16.00; and 24 and 31 December 10.00-14.00. It is closed on Mondays, on 1 May and on 25 December.

places.name: Torre della Moletta
places.summary: A medieval tower inside the Circus Maximus archaeological complex, also called Turris in Capite Circi or Turris de Arco and named for a mill driven by the water of the Fosso di San Giovanni. Square in plan, built of small tufa blocks with chips of limestone and flint and irregular brick courses. An internal stair now reaches the upper floor, a viewpoint over the archaeological area.
places.history: Property of the Frangipane from at least 1145. The tower stood among modest structures and belonged to a system of fortifications demolished in 1943; the ancient masonry was later restored and consolidated. Turismo Roma records that 1930s excavations brought up much of the hemicycle and the remains of the Arco di Tito at this end of the circus, and that investigations concluded in 2016 by Roma Capitale and the Sovrintendenza Capitolina, with technical support from Zetema Progetto Cultura, opened new visitor routes with lighting.

places.name: Mitreo del Circo Massimo
places.address: Via dell'Ara Massima, Roma RM
places.summary: A mithraeum beneath a building on via dell'Ara Massima, in the ground between the Circus Maximus and the Forum Boarium. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: It is also called the Mitreo Pantanella, because it came to light during the 1930s demolition and clearance works around the Pantanella plant.

places.name: Ex Pastificio Pantanella
places.address: Via dei Cerchi, Roma RM
places.summary: The former pasta works on via dei Cerchi, along the Circus Maximus. Since 1931 the rear of the building, facing the circus, has held the costume and scenery stores and some technical services of the Teatro dell'Opera di Roma. It now also houses Roma Capitale's Dipartimento Sviluppo Economico, Attivita Produttive e Agricoltura.
places.history: Built between 1878 and 1881 on the initiative of Michelangelo Pantanella, to designs by the engineer Pio Scarselli, to hold the offices and ovens of the Societa dei Molini e Pastificio Pantanella; at the time the whole Circus Maximus valley still held industrial plant, including the gasworks. The firm moved to via Casilina in 1929 and the works were restructured as the Palazzo dei Musei di Roma, housing the Museo dell'Impero romano, opened 9 June 1929, and the Museo della Citta di Roma, opened 21 April 1930. The building closed in 1939 and in 1952 the two collections went to the Museo della civilta romana at EUR and the Museo di Roma at Palazzo Braschi.

places.name: Rhinoceros - Fondazione Alda Fendi
places.address: Via del Velabro 9, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A gallery on via del Velabro, established in Rome by Alda Fendi, with a restaurant and apartments in the same complex. Contacts, from its own site: gallery +39 340 6430435 and gallery@rhinocerosroma.com, apartments hospitality@rhinocerosroma.com, restaurant eventi@retro-bottega.com. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The operating company is Agrippina S.R.L.

places.name: Monumento a Giuseppe Mazzini
places.address: Piazzale Ugo La Malfa, Roma RM
places.summary: A bronze and marble monument on piazzale Ugo La Malfa, on the Aventine slope facing the Circus Maximus, by the sculptor Ettore Ferrari. A high quadrangular base carries a continuous high-relief frieze 27 m long on three sides; the rear drum bears medallions of Pisacane, Mameli, Campanella, Saffi, Quadrio, Alberto Mario and Jessie White, Rosolino Pilo and Adriano Lemmi. The seated bronze Mazzini on top is 5 m tall.
places.history: Proposed to the Chamber of Deputies in 1887 and again in 1890 under Crispi; the commission went to Ferrari in 1902, he presented a maquette in 1905, and in 1911 he removed the Doric tempietto that would have crowned it. The revised design was approved in 1914 with the Aventine slope chosen as its site and the first stone was laid in 1922, but work slowed under Fascism's hostility to Freemasonry, Ferrari and Mazzini both being Masons. At Ferrari's death in 1929 the statues and groups were finished. In 1934 the new via del Circo Massimo opened with piazzale Romolo e Remo, today piazzale Ugo La Malfa, where the broad travertine-benched exedra around the future monument was built. Work resumed in 1948 under the sculptor's son Gian Giacomo Ferrari and the sculptor Ettore Guastalla, and the monument was inaugurated on 2 June 1949, the centenary of the Roman Republic of 1849. It was restored in 1999 and 2000.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Sabina all'Aventino
places.address: Piazza Pietro d'Illiria 1, Roma RM
places.summary: The Dominican basilica on the Aventine, entered through an atrium on four antique marble and four granite columns that gathers stone fragments, imperial-era sarcophagi and remains of ancient screens. The central portal has a classical marble surround and cypress-wood doors carved in relief with Old and New Testament scenes; the interior runs on twenty-four fluted Corinthian columns. Visiting: Sunday and Monday 12.00-19.00, Tuesday to Saturday 08.00-19.00, with days of precept running as Sundays. Entry is free and no booking is needed. Visits are not permitted during liturgical celebrations. The excavations are not accessible.
places.history: Founded in 425 by Peter, a priest of Illyria, on an earlier Titulus Sabinae, and restored by Leo III and then Eugene II, who added the schola cantorum. In the tenth century its command of the river made it a fortified residence, of the Crescenzi and then the Savelli. In 1219 Honorius III gave the church and part of the palace to St Dominic, founder of the Dominicans, who lived and worked here; the campanile and cloister date from then. Domenico Fontana transformed it for Sixtus V in 1587, and in the early twentieth century Antonio Munoz stripped the Baroque additions and returned it to its medieval appearance. Of the original fifth-century decoration only a great mosaic band survives, with an inscription in gold letters on blue naming Peter of Illyria and Pope Celestine I. To the right of the wooden door a small column marks where St Dominic is said to have prayed at night, topped by a black basalt stone, probably a Roman weight.

places.name: Giardino degli Aranci (Parco Savello)
places.address: Piazza Pietro d'Illiria, Roma RM
places.summary: A walled rectangular garden of about 7,800 m2 on the Aventine, laid out inside the ground of the Savelli fortress, whose medieval walls enclose it. It is symmetrical about a central axis aligned on the belvedere over the river, which gives a view from the Tiber bend to St Peter's. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The fortress was of the late thirteenth century, raised in turn on a tenth-century Crescenzi castle. Of the thirteenth-century castle only some granaries and underground stores remain, the building itself having been almost entirely demolished in 1613; the traces of its towers and drawbridge are legible in the enclosing wall opposite Santa Sabina's flank and apse, which also carries marks of a late-sixteenth-century intervention by Domenico Fontana for Sixtus V. The park was laid out in 1932 to the design of the architect Raffaele De Vico. The orange trees that give it its name commemorate St Dominic, who founded the convent here in the thirteenth century; the orange tree by which he preached is kept in the cloister of Santa Sabina and is still visible through a hole in the wall of the church portico.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi Bonifacio e Alessio all'Aventino
places.address: Piazza di Sant'Alessio, Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica on piazza di Sant'Alessio, entered through a medieval four-sided portico, with three naves on piers with fluted pilasters and Corinthian capitals. Against the inner facade, in a glass case held by angels and putti, is the wooden staircase under which St Alexis is said to have lived. The Romanesque crypt holds relics of St Thomas Becket and a column said to be the one to which St Sebastian was bound. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Built between the third and fourth centuries and dedicated at first to St Boniface; in 986 St Alexis was added to the title. It was rebuilt in 1217, when the relics of the two saints were placed under the high altar. The present appearance comes from works begun before the 1750 jubilee to the design of Giovanni Battista Nolli, 1701 to 1756, reworked by Tommaso De Marchis, 1693 to 1759, with further work between 1852 and 1860 by the Somaschi Fathers, to whom Pius IX had given the basilica. De Marchis's facade is neo-cinquecentesco; to its right stands the thirteenth-century campanile of five orders with paired bifore, and the cloister has granite columns taken from ancient buildings. Michele Ottaviani painted the vault of the central nave, and Carlo Gavardini the apse and the crossing pendentives.

places.name: Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta
places.address: Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta, Roma RM
places.summary: The square on the Aventine crest onto which the priory of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, its church of Santa Maria del Priorato and the abbey of Sant'Anselmo all open. Turismo Roma's Aventine itinerary begins here.
places.history: Turismo Roma credits the square's present appearance to Giovanni Battista Piranesi, who designed the piazza in front of the priory alongside his work on the church, commissioned in 1764 by Cardinal Giovanni Battista Rezzonico.

places.name: Villa del Priorato di Malta
places.address: Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta 3-4, Roma RM
places.summary: Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta 3-4, on the Aventine. The complex of buildings and garden is the historic seat of the Grand Priory of Rome of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta and houses the Order's embassy to the Italian State. The hole in the portal at number 3 frames, at the end of an avenue of trees, the dome of St Peter's.
places.history: The keyhole is visible from the square, which is public ground. No source states visiting arrangements for the villa or its garden, so none are given here.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Priorato
places.address: Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta 4, Roma RM
places.summary: The church of the Sovereign Order of Malta on the Aventine, with a single-order facade of four fluted pilasters with rich capitals and a portal under an oculus and triangular tympanum. Latin-cross interior with side niches and an apse under a stuccoed vault. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: In 1761 Giovanni Battista Piranesi dedicated his treatise Della Magnificenza ed Architettura dei Romani to the Rezzonico; in 1764 Cardinal Giovanni Battista Rezzonico, formerly Grand Prior of the Order, commissioned him to renew the church, the villa gardens and the piazza in front. In 1765 Piranesi recast it in the neoclassical manner as a funerary chamber honouring the Grand Priors and Grand Masters of the Order, mixing Egyptian, Etruscan and Roman iconography: sarcophagus, serpent, skull, inverted torches, with the crowned double-headed eagle of the Rezzonico arms. A restoration in 2017 recovered the original colour, white stuccoes and a soft ochre, by removing dust, deposits and candle soot.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Anselmo all'Aventino e Badia Primaziale
places.address: Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta, Roma RM
places.summary: A church which, with its attached monastery, forms the Badia Primaziale of the Benedictine order, on the Aventine, at piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta. The Divine Office is sung in Latin with traditional Gregorian chant, with daily Mass and monthly adoration. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Collegio's own site records that Sant'Anselmo is the seat of the Benedictine Confederation and holds the Curia of the Abbot Primate, and that about 90 monks and religious from over 30 countries live here, studying at the Ateneo or at other Roman universities. The Pontifical Athenaeum of Sant'Anselmo, built between 1892 and 1900, stands in the same complex.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Prisca
places.address: Via di Santa Prisca 11, Roma RM
places.summary: A parish church on the Aventine, standing where tradition puts the earliest Christian worship on the hill. Mass times as Turismo Roma publishes them: in winter, weekdays 08.00 and 18.00, Sundays and feasts 08.00, 10.30, 12.00 and 18.00; in summer, weekdays 08.00 and 19.00, Sundays and feasts 08.00, 10.30 and 19.00. Telephone 06 5743798.
places.history: The site is identified with the titulus Aquilae et Priscillae, the parents of St Prisca, who by tradition was baptised by St Peter at thirteen and martyred in the first century; the same tradition places both Peter and Paul here. In the third century, under Pope Eutychian, her body was found and the site dedicated to her. The hagiography has her imprisoned under Claudius for refusing to venerate Apollo, scourged and condemned to the beasts in the Circus Maximus, where the lions lay at her feet; thrown on a pyre and unharmed, she was finally beheaded at the tenth milestone of the via Ostiense. After several restorations, one following the devastation by Robert Guiscard's Normans in 1084, the church took its present form in 1599.

places.name: Mitreo di Santa Prisca
places.address: Via di Santa Prisca 8, Roma RM
places.summary: A mithraeum beneath the church of Santa Prisca: a long rectangular main room for the ritual banquet, preceded by two niches that held Cautes and Cautopates, the mithraic genii of dawn and dusk, of which only the marble Cautes with raised torch survives. In the end wall a large niche holds Mithras killing the bull and a reclining Saturn built of amphora fragments faced in gilded stucco; the side walls are frescoed with the sacred procession of the cult's servants bearing offerings, and another niche is decorated with seven concentric circles for the planetary spheres. Turismo Roma states that visits are temporarily suspended and advises checking the official site.
places.history: Found by chance in 1934 by the Augustinian Fathers. It was built into the walls of two earlier buildings, one of the late first century AD and one of the second with two aisles, over which the church was later raised. The mithraeum itself dates to the third century AD, and an inscription shows it was already in use in AD 202. It was violently destroyed around AD 400, probably by Christians, before the church was built.

places.name: Roseto di Roma Capitale
places.address: Clivo dei Publicii 3 / Via di Valle Murcia 6, Roma RM
places.summary: The municipal rose garden on the Aventine slope above the Circus Maximus, holding about 1,100 species of rose from around the world, among them Rosa chinensis viridiflora with green petals, Rosa chinensis mutabilis, which changes colour over days, and the ill-smelling Rosa foetida. The lower and smaller section holds the roses entered for the Premio Roma and the collection of past winners. Turismo Roma states that the Roseto generally opens for the spring flowering from late April into May and again in October, with the calendar set each year.
places.history: The ground has been given to flowers since the third century BC: Tacitus records in the Annales a temple of the goddess Flora, whose floralia were held in spring in the Circus Maximus. It lay under gardens and vineyards through the sixteenth century, and in 1645 became the Orto degli Ebrei, with a small cemetery for the Jewish community. From 1934, when that cemetery was moved to the Verano, the city plan designated the area a park; it lay uncultivated until 1950, when it became the new municipal rose garden. In thanks to the Jewish community for allowing the garden on a sacred site, a stele recording the earlier use was placed at the entrance, and the paths dividing the beds in the collection area were laid out in the shape of the menorah. The Premio Roma has run since its first edition, in 1933 on the Colle Oppio.

places.name: Scatola Archeologica di Piazza Albania
places.address: Piazza Albania, Roma RM
places.summary: A covered excavation on piazza Albania, on the Aventine, visited by booking. No concrete opening hours are published, so none are given here.
places.history: Its own site records that the earliest evidence on the site goes back to the foundation of Rome in the eighth century BC, and that between the sixth and third centuries BC a tufa-block wall was built, read as a watchtower inside the fortifications, whose monumental remains are visible today at piazza Albania and in via di Sant'Anselmo. A late-third-century-BC intervention raised the ground level with earth and debris that yielded a great deal of contemporary ceramic. By the mid-second century BC a domus began to develop inside a massive opus incertum wall, turning the area from military to residential use; living quarters, food-storage rooms and water-disposal systems have been identified, and six superimposed floor levels from the first century BC to the second century AD record successive owners, perhaps merchants engaged in the Tiber Emporium trade. Some of the rebuilding appears linked to unstable subsoil, cut through by quarries for tufa and pozzolana.

places.name: Terme Deciane e Casale Torlonia
places.address: Piazza del Tempio di Diana, Roma RM
places.summary: The remains of a bath complex on the Aventine, lying beneath piazza del Tempio di Diana and beneath the Casale Torlonia, which incorporates some of them. No source states visiting arrangements, so none are given here.
places.history: The baths were built by the emperor Decius in AD 249, from whom they take their name, and served the wealthy clientele of the Aventine.

places.name: Arco di San Lazzaro
places.address: Via Marmorata, Roma RM
places.summary: A Roman-era arch on via Marmorata. No source states visiting arrangements, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records it as an arch of Roman date standing in the rione Ripa.

places.name: Isola Tiberina
places.summary: The island in the Tiber, about 300 m long and 90 m wide, joined to the banks by two bridges: ponte Cestio to Trastevere, of about 46 BC, and ponte Fabricio, of 62 BC, also called ponte Quattro Capi for the Roman herms on its parapets. It is Ripa's: it.wikipedia's article on the rione states that the Isola Tiberina belongs to Ripa.
places.history: Legend has the island forming in 509 BC, when the people, having deposed Tarquinius Superbus, threw the king's grain store into the river in such quantity that it made an islet; geologically it rests on a compact tufa bank akin to the Capitoline's, on which the current's sands settled. Another legend: in 291 BC, during a plague, priests consulted the Sibylline books and sent a delegation to Epidaurus, cult site of Asclepius, and the envoys returned with a serpent, which leapt ashore here, so that a temple to Aesculapius was raised where it took refuge. The island was then shaped architecturally as a ship, with stern and prow and an obelisk amidships for the mast, and the travertine revetment of the prow survives at the downstream end. The church of San Bartolomeo all'Isola later rose on the Roman temple's remains, and the island's medical vocation continues with the Fatebenefratelli hospital and the Ospedale Israelitico.

places.name: Basilica di San Bartolomeo all'Isola
places.address: Piazza di San Bartolomeo all'Isola, Roma RM
places.summary: The basilica on the Isola Tiberina, with a two-storey Baroque facade and portico, an interior of three naves on antique columns, a twelfth-century Romanesque campanile and a hollowed column used as a wellhead. It holds the remains of the apostle St Bartholomew in a red porphyry sarcophagus under the high altar, and those of St Adalbert, bishop of Prague, killed in 997; among the works inside is the Flagellation of Christ by Antonio Carracci, 1589 to 1618, nephew of Annibale. The Comunita di Sant'Egidio, which runs it, presents it as the sanctuary and Memoriale of the new martyrs of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries; the Memoriale dei Nuovi Martiri opens on Saturday 09.30-13.30 and 15.30-17.30, and otherwise by booking through the basilica.
places.history: Built at the end of the tenth century at the will of the emperor Otto III over an ancient temple of Aesculapius, and first dedicated to St Adalbert; much restored between the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Irreparably damaged by a Tiber flood in 1557, it was rebuilt in the seventeenth century by the architect Orazio Torriani. It was the seat of the Veneranda confraternita de' devoti di Gesu Cristo al Calvario e di Maria Santissima Addolorata, formed in 1760, which obtained permission from Pius VI to make a cemetery for its dead in the basement; its members wore a red hooded cloak, hence the popular name Sacconi Rossi. From the outset they recovered bodies found in the Tiber, whose bones were laid in the crypt.

places.name: Ospedale Isola Tiberina - Gemelli Isola
places.address: Via di Ponte Quattro Capi 39, Roma RM
places.summary: A working hospital on the Isola Tiberina, founded by the Hospitaller Order of St John of God, whose friars are called Fatebenefratelli, the name by which Romans know it. It is not a visitor site.
places.history: It stands on the site of the ancient temple to Aesculapius. Turismo Roma dates the foundation of the hospital to 1584. Since 1 September 2022 it has carried the name Ospedale Isola Tiberina - Gemelli Isola, after purchase by Gemelli Isola - Societa Benefit S.p.A., created by the Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS.

places.name: Oratorio di Gesu al Calvario e di Maria (Sacconi Rossi)
places.summary: A deconsecrated oratory on the Isola Tiberina, also called Santa Maria Addolorata dei Sacconi Rossi. It was the oratory of the old Franciscan monastery north of San Bartolomeo all'Isola, dedicated to Jesus at Calvary and Our Lady of Sorrows, and a subsidiary church of the parish of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli. It has been deconsecrated since 1988.
places.history: Every All Saints' Day the Sacconi Rossi went to the point of the island facing Ponte Rotto and cast a wreath into the river in memory of the drowned whose bodies were never found. The custom is now carried on by the Fatebenefratelli and the confraternity of Santa Maria dell'Orto.

places.name: Ponte Fabricio
places.summary: The bridge linking the Isola Tiberina to the left bank, built in 62 BC and still in use. Two large slightly depressed arches rest on a central pier pierced by a relieving arch to reduce flood pressure; the construction is in cementizio with squared Gabine stone and tufa, faced over much of its length in travertine, and the brickwork belongs to the seventeenth-century repairs. Turismo Roma names Sant'Angelo as the rione the bridge reaches on the left bank.
places.history: It replaced an earlier timber bridge already standing in 192 BC, per Livy. Four large inscriptions on the arches name the builder, Lucius Fabricius, then curator viarum, and a smaller one records repairs by Marcus Lollius and Quintus Lepidus in the first century BC after two Tiber floods; Horace remembers it as a place from which the desperate threw themselves. Eugene IV paved it in travertine slabs in 1447, and Innocent XI consolidated the structure and remade the parapets in 1679. The parapet carries four-fronted marble herms, whence the modern name Ponte dei Quattro Capi, attested by the early sixteenth century; popular legend makes the herms four architects commissioned by Sixtus V to restore the bridge, who quarrelled and were beheaded on the spot at the end of the works. When the Jewish community occupied the area on the left bank the bridge was also called dei Giudei.

places.name: Ponte Cestio
places.summary: The bridge from the Isola Tiberina to Trastevere, built around 46 BC, probably by Lucius Cestius, left by Caesar to govern Rome during the Spanish war. Its span and far abutment lie in Trastevere; the island abutment is Ripa's. It stands as three large arches faced in the original travertine.
places.history: Repeatedly repaired against the current, it was rebuilt in 365 by Valentinian, Valens and Gratian as one great arch flanked by two smaller. In AD 370 it was called di Graziano, per the inscription in the upstream parapet; later San Bartolomeo, from the island's principal church; later still ferrato, from the iron chains needed to anchor floating mills on barges, a technique that became essential to Rome's flour supply after 537, when Vitiges cut the aqueducts driving the Tiber mills. It was damaged in the French invasion of 1849 but little changed in appearance, and was dismantled and rebuilt when the riverbed was widened for the new embankments.

places.name: Ponte Rotto (Ponte Emilio)
places.summary: A single mid-stream pier standing in the Tiber, all that survives of the Pons Aemilius. It is the object Romans call Ponte Rotto, the broken bridge.
places.history: The Pons Aemilius crossed the Tiber upstream of the ancient Pons Sublicius. A single mid-stream pier survives. It was earlier called Ponte di S. Maria or Senatorio, and the Crescenzi levied a toll on its traffic.

places.name: Ponte Palatino
places.summary: A road bridge of five spans on four massive masonry piers faced in travertine bossage, carrying a metal deck that lands at each end in the embankment walls raised after the flood of 1870. It is just over 155 m long and about 19 m wide, and joins Lungotevere Ripa to Lungotevere Aventino; Turismo Roma says it lies in the rioni Ripa and Trastevere. The Cloaca Maxima, still working, discharges on the left side at lungotevere Aventino.
places.history: Built between 1886 and 1890 to the design of the engineer Angelo Vescovali, with a Belgian firm specialising in iron bridges and the Officina dell'Impresa Industriale Italiana for the metalwork, to serve the crossing the Pons Aemilius had once carried. It is a plain structure without the great arches of most Roman bridges and without heavy ornament apart from the metal lattice with lozenge elements joining its sections. Romans once held the partita a rocci, or sassaiola, the mass stone-throwing between the men of Testaccio and Trastevere, on this bridge.

places.name: Trattoria Sora Lella
places.summary: A Roman trattoria on the Isola Tiberina. Its own site gives lunch Monday to Saturday 12.30-14.50 and dinner Monday to Saturday 19.20-22.50, closed Sunday, with bookings by telephone and a stated dress code.
places.history: The trattoria describes its cooking as traditional Roman.

places.name: Kolbe Hotel Rome
places.address: Via di San Teodoro 48, Roma RM
places.summary: A hotel at Via di San Teodoro 48. Its own site establishes the name and the address, and no source states more.
places.history: No source states its history, so none is given here.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Cosmedin
entries.note: A diaconia first recorded in the sixth century, enlarged in 782 over the Ara Maxima of Hercules, with a 34.20 m campanile carrying a bell of 1289.

entries.name: Bocca della Verita
entries.note: The pierced marble face, about 1.80 m across and probably a Roman drain cover, set in the basilica's pronaos since 1632; the name dates from 1485.

entries.name: Arco degli Argentari
entries.note: A trabeated gateway of AD 204 paid for by the money-changers and cattle merchants, with Geta and Plautilla chiselled off the dedicatory inscription.

entries.name: Circo Massimo
entries.note: The chariot circus in the Valle Murcia, 600 m by 140 m, rebuilt almost entirely under Trajan; the archaeological area opens Tuesday to Sunday.

entries.name: Circo Maximo Experience
entries.note: An augmented- and virtual-reality route of about 40 minutes with nine stops, in eight languages, tickets 12.00 euro full and 10.00 euro reduced.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Sabina all'Aventino
entries.note: Founded in 425 by Peter of Illyria, given to St Dominic in 1219, with carved cypress doors and twenty-four fluted Corinthian columns. Entry is free.

entries.name: Giardino degli Aranci (Parco Savello)
entries.note: About 7,800 m2 of walled garden inside the Savelli fortress ground, laid out in 1932 by Raffaele De Vico, with a belvedere over the river.

entries.name: Villa del Priorato di Malta
entries.note: The hole in the portal at Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta 3 frames, at the end of an avenue of trees, the dome of St Peter's.

entries.name: Isola Tiberina
entries.note: About 300 m by 90 m, shaped in antiquity as a ship with stern, prow and an obelisk for a mast, and still carrying the island's medical vocation.

entries.name: Basilica di San Bartolomeo all'Isola
entries.note: Built at the end of the tenth century for Otto III over a temple of Aesculapius; the Memoriale dei Nuovi Martiri opens on Saturday mornings and afternoons.

entries.name: Ponte Fabricio
entries.note: Built in 62 BC by Lucius Fabricius and still in use; its four-fronted marble herms give it the name Ponte dei Quattro Capi.

entries.name: Roseto di Roma Capitale
entries.note: About 1,100 rose species on paths laid out in the shape of the menorah; Turismo Roma gives the opening as the spring flowering and again in October.

entries.name: Trattoria Sora Lella
entries.note: Roman cooking on the Isola Tiberina; lunch 12.30-14.50 and dinner 19.20-22.50 Monday to Saturday, closed Sunday, bookings by telephone.

entries.name: Kolbe Hotel Rome
entries.note: A hotel at Via di San Teodoro 48, whose own site establishes its name and its address.

The neighbour at piazza di Monte Savello, which ponte Fabricio reaches on the left bank; it holds the Portico d'Ottavia and the Teatro di Marcello.
Across the river, reached from the island by ponte Cestio and sharing ponte Palatino.
The neighbour beyond via Marmorata and piazza dell'Emporio, carved out of Ripa in 1921.
The neighbour beyond viale Aventino and piazza Albania, carved out of Ripa in 1921; it holds the Baths of Caracalla.
The neighbour beyond piazza di Porta Capena, and the rione the Colosseum stands in.
The three-day Rome itinerary in this series. The Circus Maximus, the Bocca della Verita and the Isola Tiberina are all inside this rione.
